subject: Critical Thinking
title: Aristotle: The First Scientist of Everything
description: A 60-second lesson on Aristotle: The First Scientist of Everything.

hook.text: Biology, physics, ethics, logic, politics, poetry, rhetoric – Aristotle didn't just study them.

buildup.text: Plato's student, Alexander the Great's tutor, founder of the Lyceum.

discovery.text: Aristotle formalized syllogisms so arguments could be tested for structure, not just style.

twist.text: Aristotle was wrong about many things (heavier objects fall faster, women have fewer teeth).

climax.text: For 2,000 years, 'Aristotle said so' ended debates.

punchline.text: Aristotle often missed the facts, but he taught the West how to reason in public.

quiz.question: What was Aristotle's greatest contribution to critical thinking?
options: Formal logic and the syllogism — the foundation of systematic reasoning

details.summary: Aristotle created the first formal system of logic, classified virtually every field of knowledge, and insisted on empirical observation as the basis for understanding nature. His syllogistic logic dominated reasoning for over two thousand years.
details.whyItMatters: Aristotle's logical framework is the scaffolding on which all Western science and philosophy was built, and his methods of classification remain foundational.
takeaways: He classified fields from biology to ethics systematically
He combined observation with logical deduction

faq.question: What is a syllogism and why did Aristotle consider it important?
faq.answer: A syllogism links two premises to a guaranteed conclusion: All men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal. Aristotle saw syllogisms as the fundamental unit of valid reasoning.

faq.question: How did Aristotle's approach differ from Plato's theory of forms?
faq.answer: Plato sought truth in abstract ideal forms beyond the physical world. Aristotle insisted on observing the physical world directly and deriving principles from what could be seen, counted, and classified.
